units.name: Case: a pairs trade that breaks
Case: a trend system from backtest to live

terms.short: Same asset, same price everywhere
terms.definition: The idea that the same thing should trade at the same price everywhere, once costs are counted. Arbitrage is what enforces it: when prices drift apart, traders buy where it's cheap and sell where it's dear until the gap closes.
examples: The futures can't stay ₹50 over fair value for long; the law of one price says someone will sell them and buy the stocks.
The analyst says the law of one price is why the ETF trades so close to its holdings.
The client asked why a stock costs the same on NSE and BSE: the law of one price, enforced by arbitrage.
terms.fill: Arbitrage traders are what enforce the ____: if the same bond is cheaper in one place, they buy it there and sell it where it's dear.
wrong: Prices always follow fundamentals
Every stock's price drifts to its average
Exchanges must quote one price

terms.short: Same stock, two exchanges, one gap
terms.definition: Buying a stock on one exchange and selling it on another when their prices differ, such as NSE and BSE. The gaps are tiny and close within moments, so it's done by fast algorithms.
examples: NSE ticked up first and BSE lagged by 40 paise; the exchange arb algo was in and out before anyone saw it.
Risk caps the exchange arbitrage book's open positions, in case one leg fails.
The client asked whether she can profit from NSE–BSE price gaps; exchange arbitrage is a game for the fastest firms.
terms.fill: An algo that buys Infosys on BSE at ₹1,500.00 and sells it on NSE at ₹1,500.50 in the same instant is doing ____.
wrong: Same index, futures against stocks
Same company, two share classes
Three currencies against each other

terms.short: ETF price against its basket's value
terms.definition: Trading the gap between an exchange-traded fund's price and the value of the shares it holds. When the ETF trades above that value, market makers sell units and buy the shares to create new ones; below it, they do the reverse. In India, only the fund's market makers and deals above ₹25 crore can create or redeem units directly with the fund house; everyone else trades on the exchange.
examples: The gold ETF is 0.5% over its iNAV, so the market maker is selling units and creating more.
The analyst says ETF arbitrage keeps the gold ETF within a whisker of its holdings' value.
Risk notes that ETF arbitrage breaks down when the underlying market is closed.
terms.fill: With the Nifty ETF trading 0.4% above the value of its shares, the market maker sold units and bought the stocks to create more: ____.
wrong: Same stock on two exchanges
Futures against the index's stocks
A stock against its takeover offer

terms.short: An ETF's live value from its holdings
terms.definition: An exchange-traded fund's indicative net asset value: what its units are worth from the live prices of the shares it holds. Exchanges show it through the trading day, at most 15 seconds old, so you can see whether the ETF trades at a premium or a discount.
examples: Don't buy the ETF blind: it's 1% over iNAV right now.
The client asked why her ETF bought above the NAV; the dealer said to compare the price with the iNAV instead.
Risk checks the iNAV before every large ETF trade.
terms.fill: During the trading day, the ETF's ____, updated every few seconds from its holdings' live prices, read 251.20 while units traded at 252.10, a premium of 0.36%.
wrong: The fund's price at yesterday's close
Value of one creation unit in rupees
The ETF's price on the exchange

calcs.q: An ETF's iNAV is 250.00 and its units trade at 251.50. What's the premium?

terms.short: Betting a takeover deal will close
terms.definition: Buying a company that's being taken over at less than the offer price and waiting for the deal to close. In a share-for-share deal the buyer's stock is sold short, or its futures sold, as a hedge. The gap is the pay for the risk that the deal fails.
examples: The spread on the takeover is 6% with four months to close; the merger arb desk thinks the regulator will clear it.
Risk sizes merger arbitrage positions by what they'd lose if the deal broke.
The client asked why her merger arbitrage fund fell when one deal was blocked.
terms.fill: The stock trades at ₹940 against a cash takeover at ₹1,000 due to close in four months, and the desk buys it, betting the deal goes through: ____.
wrong: Same stock on two exchanges
ETF price against its basket
Long winners, short losers

calcs.q: A target trades at ₹940 and the cash offer is ₹1,000, closing in about 4 months. What's the return over those four months if the deal closes?
calcs.why: You make ₹60 on ₹940: 60 ÷ 940 ≈ 6.4% over the four months, about 19% a year.

tf.s: A merger arbitrage trade can lose far more than it stands to make.
tf.why: If the deal breaks, the price can fall back to where it was before the offer, often much further than the gap to the offer price.

terms.short: Three currency rates that don't line up
terms.definition: Trading three currency pairs when one cross rate doesn't match the rate implied by the other two, such as EUR/INR against EUR/USD and USD/INR. Banks' systems close such gaps almost at once.
examples: EUR/INR was a few paise off the cross for a moment, and the bank's triangular arb engine took it.
Risk asked how the triangular arbitrage engine handles a quote that turns out to be stale.
The analyst says triangular arbitrage keeps the rupee crosses lined up within a few paise.
terms.fill: With USD/INR at 88.00 and EUR/USD at 1.1600, EUR/INR should be 102.08. Quoted at 102.40, the desk sold euros for rupees and bought them back through dollars: ____.
wrong: Borrow a cheap currency, buy a dear one
Same stock on two exchanges
Hedge a dollar receivable with futures

calcs.q: USD/INR is 88.00 and EUR/USD is 1.1600. What EUR/INR rate leaves no gap?
calcs.why: Rupees per euro = rupees per dollar × dollars per euro: 88.00 × 1.16 = 102.08.

terms.short: Many small hedged bets, each with an edge
terms.definition: Running many small long and short positions at once, each with a slight statistical edge, such as related stocks drifting back together, with market risk hedged out. No single trade is sure; the edge shows up across thousands of them.
examples: The stat arb book runs 400 names, beta-neutral, and turns over every few days.
Risk watches the statistical arbitrage book for crowding, since many funds hold similar bets.
The client asked what statistical arbitrage means: many small bets, each with a slight edge.
terms.fill: Running 300 small long-short stock bets at once, each with a slight edge and the market hedged out, is ____.
wrong: One trade with a locked-in profit
Same stock on two exchanges
Buying a takeover target

tf.s: Statistical arbitrage locks in a profit on every trade.
tf.why: Each trade only has better-than-even odds. The profit comes from the average over many trades, and losing runs happen.

terms.short: Why price gaps can persist
terms.definition: The reasons price gaps can last: trading costs, the margin and capital a trade ties up, rules on short selling, and the risk that the gap widens before it closes. They're why a mispricing isn't always free money.
examples: The ADR premium is huge, but you can't short the Indian leg cheaply; limits to arbitrage.
The analyst says limits to arbitrage explain why the holding company trades at a deep discount.
Risk reminds the desk that limits to arbitrage can make a mispricing get worse before it closes.
terms.fill: The futures sat 1% below fair value for weeks because shorting the stocks was hard and margin was tight, a textbook case of the ____.
wrong: Rules capping how much one fund can own
Exchange limits on daily price moves
Cap on the number of open positions

tf.s: If a price gap lasts for weeks, there can't be any arbitrage traders in that market.
tf.why: They may be there but held back by costs, capital, margin or short-selling rules, or by the risk that the gap widens first.

terms.short: One side fills, the other doesn't
terms.definition: The risk in a trade with several parts that one part fills and another doesn't, or fills at a worse price, leaving an open position instead of a hedged one.
examples: We got the buy on BSE but the NSE sell missed; leg risk left us long 2,000 shares.
Risk caps leg risk by sending both orders together and cancelling if one misses.
The client asked why her spread trade lost money: one side filled and the other didn't, which is leg risk.
terms.fill: The algo bought on BSE, but its NSE sell order missed as the price moved, leaving it long: the trade's ____ had come true.
wrong: Risk that a stock is delisted
Risk of holding too many positions
Risk that the exchange halts trading

terms.short: Positions held minutes to days
terms.definition: Systematic trading that holds positions for roughly minutes to a few days, on signals such as short-term momentum, mean reversion or order flow. Speed matters less than in HFT, and trading costs and capacity matter more.
examples: We're an MFT shop: hold for hours, sometimes overnight, and never fight for microseconds.
Risk says medium-frequency trading needs low costs more than raw speed.
The client asked what medium-frequency trading is: holding positions for minutes to days.
terms.fill: Their models hold positions for a few hours to two days, and an extra millisecond of speed doesn't matter: that's ____.
wrong: Positions held for microseconds
Positions held for months
Trades placed by hand

terms.short: Positions held weeks to months
terms.definition: Systematic trading that holds positions for weeks to months, such as trend following or factor portfolios. It can run much more money than faster styles, but each signal is weaker and takes longer to prove.
examples: The LFT book rebalances monthly, so a slow broker doesn't matter but costs per trade still do.
The PM runs low-frequency trading, rebalancing once a month.
Risk notes that low-frequency trading makes few bets a year, so luck matters for longer.
terms.fill: The fund rebalances its factor portfolio once a month and holds most stocks for a quarter, a style called ____.
wrong: Positions held for seconds
Positions held for minutes to days
Buying and holding for decades

terms.short: How long a position is usually kept
terms.definition: How long a strategy typically keeps a position, from under a second in high-frequency trading to months in slower styles. It sets the costs, the capacity, and how fast you learn whether the strategy works.
examples: Stretch the holding period to a week and the costs halve, but so does the number of bets.
The client asked what the fund's holding period is: about six months per stock.
Risk checks the holding period against how fast the signal fades.
terms.fill: Moving from intraday signals to a ten-day ____ cut the strategy's trading costs by 80%.
wrong: How fast a signal's edge fades
Time from data in to order out
Days until a futures contract expires

terms.short: How fast a signal's edge fades
terms.definition: How fast a signal's edge fades: within seconds or days as prices catch up, or over months and years as more traders find and crowd it. Fast-decaying signals have to be traded quickly or not at all.
examples: The order-flow signal is worth 3 bp in the first second and nothing after ten; that's brutal alpha decay.
The quant measures alpha decay to decide how fast the signal must be traded.
Risk asked why returns fell: alpha decay, as other funds found the same signal.
terms.fill: The news signal earns 20 basis points in the first minute and almost nothing after five, showing steep ____.
wrong: How long a position is usually kept
Losses from a bad run of trades
The drop in an option's time value

terms.short: Most money a strategy can run
terms.definition: The most money a strategy can run before its own trading moves prices enough to eat its edge. Faster strategies usually have less of it; slow ones in deep markets can run far more.
examples: The signal is great but tiny: capacity is maybe ₹20 crore before impact eats it.
The PM closed the fund to new money because strategy capacity was nearly used up.
The client asked why her favourite small cap fund closed to new money: its strategy capacity was full.
terms.fill: Beyond ₹50 crore, the book's own orders moved prices and the profits shrank: it had hit its ____.
wrong: How fast a signal's edge fades
Margin a broker allows on an account
Most positions an exchange lets you hold

terms.short: Share of a portfolio traded per period
terms.definition: How much a portfolio trades over a period, as a share of its size. High turnover means high costs, so the strategy's edge has to beat them.
examples: Turnover is 40 times a year, so every basis point of cost is 40 bp of return.
The client asked why her active fund costs more than its fee: high turnover adds trading costs.
Risk caps turnover so costs don't eat the fund's edge.
terms.fill: Trading three times the portfolio's value each month gives a monthly ____ of 300%, so costs matter a lot.
wrong: How long a position is usually kept
Total profit over a year
Money flowing into the fund

calcs.q: A ₹100 crore strategy trades ₹2,500 crore a year, and each rupee traded costs 0.05% all in. Yearly cost as a share of capital?
calcs.why: ₹2,500 crore × 0.05% = ₹1.25 crore, which is 1.25% of ₹100 crore.

terms.short: Time from market data in to order out
terms.definition: The time from a market data update arriving to your order going out in response. It's the speed high-frequency firms race on, measured in microseconds or less.
examples: Tick-to-trade is 800 nanoseconds on the FPGA path and 6 microseconds in software.
Risk asked what our tick-to-trade is on the backup servers.
The quant cut tick-to-trade by moving the strategy onto the FPGA.
terms.fill: After moving its logic onto FPGA cards, the firm's ____ fell from 5 microseconds to under 1.
wrong: Time a position is usually held
Time between two trades in a stock
Delay before an exchange shows a trade

terms.short: Risk from the position a market maker builds
terms.definition: A market maker's risk from the position it builds up while quoting: if sellers keep hitting its bid, it ends up long just as the price falls. Market makers limit it by capping their position and moving both quotes to attract trades that cut it.
examples: We're long 40 lots from the morning, so skew the quotes down: inventory risk, not a view.
Risk limits inventory risk by capping how many lots the market maker can hold.
The client asked why market makers widen quotes after a big trade: inventory risk.
terms.fill: To limit her ____, the market maker caps her position at 50 lots and lowers both quotes whenever she's long.
wrong: Risk of trading with someone better informed
Risk that a quote is filled late
Risk the exchange changes the tick size

terms.short: Ride each market's own trend
terms.definition: Buying markets that have been rising and selling ones that have been falling, judged on each market's own past returns, and holding until the trend turns. It loses small amounts often and makes most of its money in a few big moves.
examples: Trend following had a rough, choppy year, then made it all back in the October sell-off.
The client asked why her trend following fund lost money in a choppy year.
Risk likes trend following in the mix, because it often makes money in long sell-offs.
terms.fill: The fund goes long any futures market above its 200-day average and short any below it, a classic ____ system.
wrong: Bet stretched prices snap back
Long one stock, short a close cousin
Rank stocks against each other

tf.s: A trend-following system usually wins on most of its trades.
tf.why: Most of its trades are small losses when trends fail. A few long trends pay for them.

terms.short: Betting stretched prices snap back
terms.definition: Betting that a price or spread that has moved far from its usual level will come back towards it: buying after sharp falls and selling after sharp rises. It works in range-bound markets and gets hurt when a real trend starts.
examples: Short-term reversal still works in mid-caps: fade the 5% gap-downs with no news.
The quant's mean reversion signal buys stocks that fell sharply on no news.
Risk warns that mean reversion bets lose big when a fall is the start of a trend.
terms.fill: Buying Infosys after a 5% fall in a day with no news, and selling a few days later as it recovers, is a ____ trade.
wrong: Ride each market's own trend
Buy what has risen most this year
Buy a takeover target

tf.s: A mean-reversion strategy does best when markets trend strongly.
tf.why: Strong trends are what hurt it: the stretched price keeps stretching. It does best in choppy, range-bound markets.

terms.short: Long one stock, short a close cousin
terms.definition: Trading two closely related stocks against each other: when the gap between them stretches unusually far, buying the cheap one and selling the dear one, then closing when the gap returns to normal. The market's moves mostly cancel out.
examples: The two cement majors have drifted apart with no news; the pairs trade says buy the laggard, sell the leader.
Risk watches pairs trading positions for a break in the link between the two stocks.
The client asked what pairs trading is: buy one stock and short a close cousin.
terms.fill: With no news, HDFC Bank fell well behind ICICI Bank, so she bought HDFC Bank futures and sold ICICI Bank futures to bet on the gap closing, a two-stock bet called ____.
wrong: Ride each market's own trend
Buying a takeover target
Same stock on two exchanges

calcs.q: You buy ₹10 lakh of stock A and sell ₹10 lakh of stock B. The market falls 3%; A falls 2% and B falls 4%. Profit or loss?
calcs.why: A loses ₹20,000 and the short in B makes ₹40,000: +₹20,000. The market's fall mostly cancels out.

terms.short: Prices tied so their spread reverts
terms.definition: When two prices that each wander freely are tied by a long-run relationship, so the spread between them keeps coming back to a stable level. It's a stronger basis for a pairs trade than correlation alone.
examples: Correlation is 0.9, but they're not cointegrated: the spread has trended for three years.
The quant tests for cointegration before adding any pair.
Risk asked whether the pair still shows cointegration after the merger news.
terms.fill: An Engle–Granger test on ten years of prices found the two banks' stocks share ____: each wanders, but their spread keeps coming back.
wrong: Daily returns that move together
A series with stable statistics
Time for half a gap to close

tf.s: Two stocks whose daily returns are highly correlated must have a spread that comes back to its average.
tf.why: Correlation is about day-to-day moves. Two stocks can move together daily and still drift apart for years; cointegration is what ties the price levels.

terms.short: Time for half a gap to close
terms.definition: How long a stretched spread or price usually takes to close half the gap back to its average. It tells you how long to expect to hold a mean-reversion trade, and when to give up on it.
examples: Half-life on this pair is about a week, so if it's still open in a month, something's changed.
Risk closes a pair if it stays open for three times its half-life.
The quant estimates the half-life from how fast the spread has reverted in the past.
terms.fill: The spread's ____ is about six days, so a trade still open after a month is probably a broken pair, not a slow one.
wrong: How long a position is usually kept
How fast a signal's edge fades
Distance from average in standard deviations

terms.short: Unaffected by the market's direction
terms.definition: Built so its value doesn't depend on which way the market moves, usually by holding equal amounts long and short with similar betas, or by hedging with index futures. Returns should come from the stock picks alone.
examples: We're market neutral, so a 5% Nifty drop barely shows; the stock picks decide our month.
The client asked whether her market neutral fund can still lose: yes, if its stock picks are wrong.
Risk checks each day that the book stays market neutral after price moves.
terms.fill: Long ₹50 crore of stocks and short ₹50 crore of others with the same beta, the fund's book is ____, so a crash shouldn't matter much.
wrong: Fully hedged against every risk
Holding only cash and bonds
Owning the whole market in one fund

terms.short: Size positions to keep risk steady
terms.definition: Sizing positions so a strategy's expected volatility stays near a set level: smaller when markets are wild, bigger when they're calm.
examples: Vol is up, so the vol target has cut us to 60% of normal size.
The client asked why her fund cut its stock holdings in the crash: volatility targeting.
Risk prefers volatility targeting, so the fund's risk stays steady whether markets are calm or wild.
terms.fill: With Nifty volatility doubling, the system halved its position to keep risk at 10% a year: ____.
wrong: Bet size that grows wealth fastest
Betting on volatility rising
Stopping trading after a loss

calcs.q: A strategy targets 10% yearly volatility. At full size its position has 25% volatility. What share of full size should it hold?
calcs.why: Target ÷ position volatility: 10% ÷ 25% = 40% of full size.

terms.short: Bet size that grows wealth fastest
terms.definition: A formula for the share of capital to stake that grows wealth fastest over time, given the edge and the odds. For an even-money bet it's the chance of winning minus the chance of losing. Traders usually stake a fraction of it, because a misjudged edge makes the full amount very risky.
examples: Full Kelly says 10%, but our edge estimate is shaky, so we run half Kelly.
Risk never lets traders bet the full Kelly criterion, because edge estimates are noisy.
The quant uses the Kelly criterion as an upper bound on position size.
terms.fill: With a 55% chance of winning an even-money bet, the ____ says to stake 10% of capital each time; most traders use half that.
wrong: Size positions to keep risk steady
Largest loss on a bad day
Return per unit of risk
terms.formula: Even-money bet: stake = p − q, the win chance minus the loss chance

calcs.q: An even-money bet wins 55% of the time. What share of capital does the full Kelly criterion stake?
calcs.why: Win chance minus loss chance: 0.55 − 0.45 = 0.10, so 10%.

tf.s: Staking twice the Kelly amount grows wealth faster than staking the Kelly amount.
tf.why: Past Kelly, extra size adds risk faster than return. At twice Kelly, long-run growth falls to about zero.

terms.short: Trade results, mergers, index changes
terms.definition: Trading around specific corporate or market events, such as results, index changes, buybacks, mergers or policy decisions, where prices tend to move in patterns around the event.
examples: Index rebalance is Friday; the event-driven desk bought the adds weeks ago and sells into the close.
Risk reviews the event-driven strategy's bets before every index rebalance.
The PM's event-driven strategy buys stocks likely to join the Nifty before they're added.
terms.fill: Trading index inclusions, buybacks and results for the price patterns around them is called ____.
wrong: Ride each market's own trend
Same stock on two exchanges
Many small hedged bets at once

terms.short: Shifting your quotes to shed inventory
terms.definition: A market maker moving both bid and ask in the direction that reduces the position: lower quotes when long so buyers come and sellers stay away, higher quotes when short. It controls inventory without leaving the market.
examples: We're long 40 lots, so the algo is skewing quotes half a tick lower until we're flat.
Quote skewing costs a little edge on each trade but stops inventory from running away.
Without quote skewing, the model kept buying into a falling market.
terms.fill: Long 40 lots, the market maker lowered both bid and ask a tick so it would sell more and buy less: ____.
wrong: Widening the spread before news
Quoting only one side of the market
Showing a smaller size than you will trade

terms.short: The share of the spread a market maker keeps
terms.definition: How much of the quoted bid-ask spread a market maker actually earns per trade after the price moves. Quoting a ₹0.10 spread and keeping ₹0.03 on average means a 30% spread capture; the rest is lost to adverse selection.
examples: Quoted spread is two ticks but spread capture is only half a tick; informed flow is eating the rest.
Spread capture fell after the new HFT entered the stock.
We measure spread capture with one-second markouts on every fill.
terms.fill: The desk quoted a two-tick spread but kept only half a tick per trade after prices moved: its ____.
wrong: The spread between two futures months
Taking the spread by crossing it
The widest spread the exchange allows

calcs.q: A market maker quotes ₹0.10 wide, so earns ₹0.05 a share against the mid when filled. One-second markouts average −₹0.03. Spread capture per share?
calcs.why: Half-spread earned (₹0.05) minus the move against you (₹0.03) leaves ₹0.02 per share.

terms.short: Where your order sits in line at a price
terms.definition: Your place among the resting orders at one price level. Under price-time priority the orders ahead of you fill first, so a good queue position decides whether a passive order fills before the price moves.
examples: We were 40,000 shares back in the queue; the offer got cleared before we filled.
HFTs cancel and requote fast to protect queue position.
Amending your order size can send you to the back of the queue, so check before you touch it.
terms.fill: Her bid was first at its price, so it filled before the 30,000 shares behind it: the value of good ____.
wrong: Your rank in the IPO allotment
The number of orders you place a second
Where a stock ranks in the index

terms.short: More size on one side of the book
terms.definition: How much more size is resting on the bid than on the offer, or the other way round, often measured at the best price as (bid − ask) ÷ (bid + ask). A strong imbalance predicts the direction of the next tick, and short-term signals use it.
examples: Order-book imbalance is +0.6: three times as much on the bid, so the next tick probably goes up.
The HFT's short-term model is mostly order-book imbalance and trade flow.
Imbalance flips fast when someone pulls a big order, so treat it as a seconds signal.
terms.fill: There was 9,000 on the bid against 3,000 on the offer, so the model expected an uptick: ____.
wrong: A gap between buy and sell volume over a day
An index with more gainers than losers
A position that is longer than it is short

calcs.q: 9,000 shares bid and 3,000 offered at the top. Order-book imbalance, (bid − ask) ÷ (bid + ask)?
calcs.why: (9,000 − 3,000) ÷ 12,000 = 0.5, a strong lean to the bid.

terms.short: The mid weighted by size at the top
terms.definition: A better short-term fair value than the plain mid: the bid and ask weighted by the size on the opposite side, (bid × ask size + ask × bid size) ÷ (bid size + ask size). It sits closer to the side with less size, the side likelier to be traded through.
examples: Mid is ₹100.025 but the microprice is ₹100.04: the bid is heavy.
Our quotes centre on the microprice, not the mid.
The microprice moved before the mid did, which is the point of it.
terms.fill: With much more size on the bid, the desk priced off the mid weighted toward the offer: the ____.
wrong: The smallest price step allowed
A price quoted for very small orders
The average price of the last few trades

terms.short: Weights so each asset adds equal risk
terms.definition: Building a portfolio so each asset class contributes the same risk, not the same money. Low-volatility assets such as bonds get bigger weights, often with leverage, and high-volatility assets such as equities get smaller ones.
examples: A 60/40 book gets about 90% of its risk from equities; risk parity evens that out.
Risk parity funds sold bonds and equities together when both fell in 2022.
Our risk parity sleeve levers bonds about 2 times.
terms.fill: Bonds were a third as volatile as equities, so the fund held about three times as much in bonds, to balance the risk: ____.
wrong: Holding the same amount of money in each asset
Matching a benchmark's sector weights
Hedging every position one for one

calcs.q: Equities have 15% vol and bonds 5%. With two assets and no correlation, what bond weight gives equal risk in a fully invested book?
calcs.why: Weights proportional to 1/vol: 1/15 and 1/5, or 1 : 3. Bonds get 3 ÷ 4 = 75%, equities 25%.

terms.short: A stock book that is long some and short others
terms.definition: A strategy that buys stocks expected to do well and shorts stocks expected to do badly, often with a modest net long. Returns come from the spread between the longs and the shorts more than from the market.
examples: Our long-short equity book runs 150% gross and 20% net.
The long-short equity fund lost on both sides when the junk rally hit.
In India, long-short equity mostly shorts through single-stock futures.
terms.fill: The fund was long 80% in quality names and short 60% in weak ones, earning mostly from the gap: ____.
wrong: Holding stocks for the long term and selling short-term
Buying calls and puts on the same stock
An index fund with a cash buffer

terms.short: Owning what pays the most to hold, everywhere
terms.definition: A systematic strategy that goes long the assets with the highest carry (the return from holding if prices don't move) and short the lowest, across currencies, bonds, commodities and equity indices. It earns steadily and can lose sharply when markets panic.
examples: The cross-asset carry book is long high-yield currencies, steep bond curves and backwardated commodities.
Cross-asset carry had a bad week as everything with high yield sold off together.
We blend cross-asset carry with trend because they tend to lose at different times.
terms.fill: The model buys whatever pays most to hold, in currencies, bonds and commodities, and shorts what pays least: ____.
wrong: Holding positions overnight to the next day
Paying a broker to carry a position forward
Rolling stock futures every month

terms.short: Patterns that repeat by calendar time
terms.definition: Return or volume patterns that repeat at the same time of the day, month or year, such as month-end flows, expiry-week behaviour, Diwali muhurat trading or the turn of the year. Quants test them carefully, because many calendar patterns are data-mined.
examples: The month-end seasonality is pension and SIP flows; it shows up in the last three days.
Volume seasonality matters for execution: the last half hour is one of the busiest of the day.
With only 20 years of Januaries, that seasonality is 20 data points; don't trust it.
terms.fill: Stocks tended to rise in the last three days of the month, as SIP and pension flows came in: a ____ effect.
wrong: A stock that only trades in some seasons
A factor that changes with the business cycle
Volatility that rises before holidays only

terms.short: Choosing weights for the best return per risk
terms.definition: Markowitz's method of picking portfolio weights that give the highest expected return for a level of risk, using expected returns, volatilities and correlations. It is very sensitive to the return estimates, so practitioners shrink inputs and add constraints.
examples: Unconstrained mean-variance optimisation put 70% in one stock; we capped names at 5%.
Small changes to expected returns flipped the mean-variance optimisation completely.
Most desks use mean-variance optimisation with shrunk covariances and turnover limits.
terms.fill: Feeding expected returns, vols and correlations into Markowitz's model to find the best weights is ____.
wrong: Averaging the returns of all stocks equally
Holding the stocks with the lowest variance only
Rebalancing a portfolio once a year

terms.short: Data beyond prices and filings
terms.definition: Data that isn't from market feeds or company reports, such as card spending, web traffic, app downloads, satellite images, GST e-way bills or job postings. Funds use it to see sales or activity before results; it is expensive, messy and its edge fades as more buy it.
examples: App download data called the food-delivery beat a month early.
Before buying alternative data, check its history is point-in-time and long enough to backtest.
Compliance has to sign off any alternative data that might contain personal information.
terms.fill: The fund bought card-spending and web-traffic numbers to forecast sales before results: ____.
wrong: Using a second data vendor for prices
Data from an alternative exchange
Estimates from sell-side analysts

terms.short: Turning raw data into model inputs
terms.definition: Building the inputs a model learns from out of raw data: ratios, changes, ranks, lags and z-scores. In finance most of the edge is in the features, and the main danger is leaking future information into them.
examples: Most of the gain came from feature engineering: ranking each signal within its sector.
A feature built from adjusted prices leaked a split from the future; fix the feature engineering.
Ten good features beat five hundred raw ones fed to a bigger model.
terms.fill: Before training the model, she turned raw prices and volumes into ranks, z-scores and lagged changes: ____.
wrong: Building the trading system's hardware
Choosing which machine-learning model to use
Writing the code that sends orders

terms.short: A forecast made by a machine-learning model
terms.definition: A trading signal produced by a machine-learning model, such as gradient-boosted trees or a neural network, trained to forecast returns from many features. In markets the data is noisy and keeps changing, so ML signals overfit easily and must be tested strictly out of sample.
examples: The ML signal had a 3.0 Sharpe in sample and 0.4 live; it was fitting noise.
Our ML signal combines 60 features with gradient-boosted trees and retrains monthly.
Before trusting an ML signal, ask what it's learned: if it can't be explained, size it small.
terms.fill: A gradient-boosted tree model trained on 60 features forecasts next-week returns: an ____.
wrong: A signal sent by a broker's market-making desk
A rule written by hand, such as a moving-average cross
An alert from the exchange's surveillance system

terms.short: Testing that removes overlap between folds
terms.definition: Cross-validation for time series that drops (purges) training data whose labels overlap the test period, and often a gap after it (an embargo). Without it, overlapping returns leak information and models look better than they are.
examples: Our labels are 20-day returns, so purged cross-validation drops 20 days either side of each test fold.
Plain k-fold showed an IC of 0.08; purged cross-validation cut it to 0.02.
Purged cross-validation is now standard on the team for any model with overlapping labels.
terms.fill: Because labels were 20-day returns, he removed the training days whose labels overlapped each test fold: ____.
wrong: Cleaning bad prices from the data
Removing outliers before training
Splitting data at random into train and test
